title: Finding deadlocks
description:
Given who holds which lock and who is waiting for which, find a deadlock (lesson 4.05), and check an acquisition sequence against a lock order:

```cpp
using Holders = std::map<std::string, std::string>;   // lock -> process holding it
using Waits = std::map<std::string, std::string>;     // process -> lock it is waiting for

std::optional<std::vector<std::string>> findDeadlock(const Holders& holders, const Waits& waits);
std::optional<std::string> orderViolation(const std::vector<std::string>& locksTaken, const std::map<std::string, int>& rank);
```

- **findDeadlock** builds the wait-for graph: a process waiting for a lock waits for that lock's holder. If there is a cycle, it returns the processes in the cycle in waiting order (each waits for the next, the last for the first), **starting with the alphabetically smallest** process in the cycle. Otherwise `std::nullopt`. A process waiting for a free lock, or for a lock held by a process that is not waiting, is not deadlocked.
- **orderViolation** takes the locks one process acquires, in order (it holds them all), and returns the first lock taken while a lock of **equal or higher** rank is already held, or `std::nullopt` if the order is respected. Locks missing from `rank` are not checked.
hints: Every process waits for at most one other process, so the wait-for graph is a set of chains. From each waiting process, follow "waits for the holder of" until you reach someone not waiting (no deadlock on this path) or someone you have already visited on this walk (a cycle).
`std::rotate` with `std::min_element` turns the cycle so that it starts at its smallest name.
